Cleanup of the shared `target/debug/deps/wmessage.db` is best-effort with `eprintln` instead of panic. When a test panics mid-way (e.g. an assertion fails before reaching `t1_cleanup(&app)` or `clean_gate_leftovers(&app)`), the seeded rows/config remain and may corrupt the next run's assertions. The comment says the next-run cleanup "begins with" a sweep that should self-heal — but `t1_cleanup` only deletes specific hard-coded ids (`t1e2e-active`, `t1e2e-done`, `job-t1e2e-active`, `T1_OWNER_ID`), so any rows inserted by partially-completed tests with different ids will leak across runs. At minimum, log a hard warning at startup if unexpected rows exist; ideally use a per-test unique namespace (UUID) so leakage can't cross tests.

`exec_never` panics with a generic message on any unexpected tool dispatch. It is correctly used as a negative assertion in 401/truncated-stream/in-stream-error paths, but the panic message (`"此路径不应执行工具：{name} {args}"`) makes debugging harder when the wrong code path dispatches a tool. More importantly, the closure-bodied `exec` for positive paths captures `Arc<Mutex<...>>` (`calls2.clone()` inside the `move`); if `exec_never` ever panics after `calls.lock().unwrap().push(...)` (or if the captured mutex is poisoned by a panic on a different path), the test outcome is `Mutex` poisoning rather than the intended assertion. Consider returning `ToolResult::err("此路径不应执行工具")` from a helper that tests assert via the surrounding error, or guard `exec_never` behind a feature flag so CI distinguishes intentional from accidental invocations.

Single-threaded sequential server: `for stream in listener.incoming()` accepts and handles connections one-at-a-time inside the spawned thread. Any test that issues concurrent requests (e.g. parallel chat-loop workers, or tests that fire two `http_post_raw` calls from different threads) will have the second connection queue at the kernel until the first fully writes+closes — this can mask genuine concurrency bugs in the client under test, produce deadlocks in tests that try to run a parallel client + server message, and silently serialize what the production code believes to be parallel traffic. Spawn a worker thread per connection (or use a thread pool) instead.

Body read can be silently truncated by the 5s read_timeout. The inner `while buf.len() < body_start + content_length` loop breaks on `Err(_)` and falls through; whatever bytes (possibly zero) were collected are then pushed into `request_bodies()`. Downstream memory-regression assertions will see corrupted/short payloads with no signal that the mock failed — and `request_count` was already incremented before the body read, so `request_count() == N` is not a sufficient sanity check. Either propagate the read error (drop the recorded body), or, if you must be permissive, log a marker when Content-Length bytes were not fully received.

Case-sensitive `Content-Length` header lookup violates RFC 7230 §3.2 (header field names are case-insensitive). Any client that emits `Content-length` (mixed case) — which some HTTP libraries do — will produce an empty `request_bodies()` entry and the request will be treated as body-less, breaking memory/contents assertions and the FragmentedTextReply path (which sends a `Content-Length` header that must match). Use a case-insensitive scan (e.g. lowercase the line before `strip_prefix`, or scan with `eq_ignore_ascii_case`).

`_handle: Option<thread::JoinHandle<()>>` is always `Some` (constructed in `start()` and never mutated), and the leading underscore plus `#[allow(dead_code)]` mean it is never used. The misleading `Option` wrapper hides the fact that the worker thread is never `join()`ed: if a test panics mid-request, or the `MockLlmServer` is dropped with a connection still open, the worker thread outlives the test (and the ephemeral port is not released until the kernel reaps it). Use plain `thread::JoinHandle<()>` and add a `Drop` impl that joins (or, given the sequential-accept note above, switches to per-connection threads and joins on drop with a timeout).

`consumed: Arc<AtomicUsize>` is a single-thread counter — it is only ever read/written inside the spawned accept thread — so the `Arc` + atomic RMW + `SeqCst` fencing is pure overhead. A `Cell<usize>` (or plain `usize` mutated under the existing `Mutex<Vec<MockBehavior>>`) suffices. `request_count` does need `Arc<AtomicUsize>` because it is observed from the test thread, but `consumed` does not.

comments.content: Every test ends with `thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50))` before asserting `request_count()`. This sleep is unnecessary: `request_count` is incremented at the top of the request handler *before* the response is written, and `http_post_raw` only returns after `read_to_string` reads EOF on the closed connection — so by the time the client returns, the server has already incremented the counter. The 50ms padding is cumulative (≥450 ms across the suite, more if CI is loaded) and provides no correctness guarantee. Either drop it entirely or replace with a bounded polling loop waiting on `request_count()` to reach the expected value (useful only if you change to per-connection threads, where the increment may race ahead).

comments.content: Cleanup failures are silently discarded via `.ok()` in both `delete_by_content` (line 71) and `cleanup_corpus` (line 78). If cleanup fails for a real reason (lock contention, schema drift, I/O error) rather than 'row not found', the start-of-test cleanup silently cannot recover, and state pollution persists across runs. The 'cleanup on panic → next run self-heals' guarantee relies on these calls actually succeeding. Consider returning `Result` and logging/propagating at least at the boundary, or wrapping cleanup in a transaction with explicit error handling.

The assertion `b.contains("已有记忆 id=")` couples the test to a localized Chinese substring of an internal prompt template. Any wording change, refactor, or i18n of the adjudication prompt turns this into a vacuous pass while real candidate-list wiring could still be broken. Prefer asserting on structural content (e.g., that the candidate IDs from `orig_ids` actually appear in some request body) so the test stays valid regardless of prompt phrasing.

The `corpus.len() * 2` LLM-call assertion combined with the pre-pushed FIFO pairing (extract → adjudicate per corpus item) tightly couples the test to an internal pipeline contract (exactly two LLM calls per item in that order). If `run_extract_with` adds, removes, or reorders a step (e.g., a clarification call), the assertion fails with confusing attribution, and a partial break (one item out of ten) only lowers the `updated >= 9` count, masking the regression. Consider asserting per-item on what each call must produce (e.g., pair extract/adjudicate bodies) rather than the aggregate call count.

`mock_handle` leaks a full `tauri::App` per invocation via `Box::leak`. Acceptable for a single test run, but if this helper is ever invoked many times (loop harness, `test-case` parametrization, or shared across other tests) the leaked apps accumulate along with stale handles that all point at the shared on-disk test DB — which can exacerbate the shared-target-dir hazard flagged in the doc comment. Consider caching a single leaked app behind a `OnceLock`/`OnceCell` (or returning a clone from a test-scoped fixture) to bound the leak.

The `extract_json` and `adjudicate_json` are built via `format!` with the corpus content/`orig_id` interpolated directly into a JSON string literal. The current corpus is well-formed so this works, but if a future corpus entry contains a quote, backslash, or control character, the mock will emit a parse-broken response and the pipeline failure will be attributed to the wrong layer. Prefer `serde_json::json!` or `serde_json::to_string` so the mock fixtures are always well-formed JSON.

TOCTOU port race in `connection_test_unreachable_reports_error`: binding `127.0.0.1:0`, capturing the port, and then immediately dropping the listener is inherently racy — another process can claim the port in the window between `drop` and the `reqwest` connect. On Linux, depending on `SO_REUSEADDR` semantics and TIME_WAIT state, the connect may also succeed against a stale socket from a previous test, making the "connect refused" assertion flaky in CI. Prefer binding a `tokio` listener (e.g. `tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")`) and using its real bound address, or pointing the probe at `http://127.0.0.1:1/` (a port reserved by IANA as `tcpmux` and almost never bound) so the unreachable precondition is guaranteed by the address itself, not by a transient race.

Asymmetric coverage: the audit-P0 regression test below specifically guards the anthropic "base without /v1" case, but there is no symmetric test for the openai provider even though the same normalization logic is exercised. A future regression where the openai branch stops prepending `/v1` would slip through this suite. Add a `connection_test_openai_base_without_v1_gets_v1_prefix` mirroring the anthropic test to enforce the invariant on both providers.

Base-URL normalization coverage is too narrow: `trim_end_matches("/v1")` only exercises the exact `…/v1` suffix. Realistic vendor URLs frequently come with trailing slashes (`…/v1/`), versioned aliases (`…/v1beta`), nested prefixes (`…/api/v1`), or query/fragment components — none of which are tested. A regression in the production normalizer (e.g. switching to a stricter prefix check) could break `verified_vendors` for users who paste the canonical `https://api.anthropic.com` (no `/v1`) plus a trailing slash, and the suite would not catch it. Extend the regression test to cover at least the trailing-slash and nested-prefix shapes, or assert the property on the production normalizer directly.

Endpoint-suffix stripping coverage is too narrow: only `/messages` (anthropic) and `/chat/completions` (openai) are exercised. Other common provider suffixes that a user might paste into Base URL — `/embeddings`, `/completions`, `/audio/speech`, `/responses`, `/images/generations` — are not tested, nor is the negative case where the suffix is NOT recognized (does the probe still reach `/v1/models`?). Also note both probe calls here share the default 200 reply; if stripping regressed for one provider and the resulting path was simply 404-able, the `r.ok` assertion would still pass against the mock. Make the second call push a non-200 behavior and assert on the recorded path explicitly per call to actually distinguish "stripped correctly" from "stripped but landed elsewhere".

Third test's cleanup is panic-unsafe and silent. The first two tests use `TraceCleanupGuard` (Drop-based) so assertion panics still trigger cleanup, but this test only runs manual `DELETE`s at function tail with `.ok()` swallowing failures. Any panic in the polling loop, `expect("trace.row...")`, or `assert!` before the cleanup block leaks rows into the shared `target/debug/deps/wmessage.db` — exactly the residue the file's own header warns about. Lift the three DELETE statements into a small `Drop` guard (or a RAII helper) that closes over `trace_id` and `handle`, mirroring the existing `TraceCleanupGuard` pattern; keep the `if let Ok(conn)` guard but also surface the first `Err` so silent DB failures don't masquerade as "nothing to clean".

`cleanup` runs nine DELETEs sequentially with no transaction and every error swallowed via `.ok()`. If `open_db` succeeds but a child-table DELETE fails (locked DB, schema drift), the parent `exec_traces` row survives and the next test inherits it through the shared `target/debug/deps/wmessage.db`. Wrap the DELETEs in `conn.transaction()` so the cascade is atomic, and at minimum log the first non-`OK` rusqlite error instead of `.ok()` so a real cleanup regression is observable rather than silent.

Polling-based synchronization for the async writer has zero diagnostics on exhaustion. If the 100×50ms loop times out under CI load, the `span_ok`/`change_ok` booleans flip to false with no record of what was observed on the last iteration, making CI flakes silent and undebuggable. Either drop a `oneshot`/notify from the writer's batch flush so the test awaits a real completion signal, or at minimum capture the last-seen `s`/`c` counts into the assertion message (`assert!(span_ok, "span missing after 5s; last s={s} c={c}")`) so a CI failure shows what the writer actually wrote (or didn't).

`Box::leak(Box::new(tauri::test::mock_app()))` is used twice (in `setup_task` and at the top of the third test) to obtain a `'static` AppHandle. Each invocation permanently leaks a `MockRuntime` and its DB handle until the test binary exits. Over a long nextest run with many tests this accumulates and can mask OS resource limits (fd / mmap) that would otherwise surface as test failures. Wrap the leaked app in a small `Drop` that performs no-op teardown and use `Box::leak` only when the lifetime must truly be `'static`; or, more practically, switch the test harness to construct the handle inside the guard so the lifetime is bounded to the guard's `Drop` (the `TraceCleanupGuard` already owns the handle — extend it to own the leaked app too).

`SERIAL` recovers from a poisoned mutex via `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`. That's intentional for tests, but it also means a panic inside one test's body (while SERIAL is held, or before its `Drop` runs cleanup) will be ignored on the next test entry and the next test will silently run against a poisoned lock — masking real concurrency regressions. Prefer `_serial = SERIAL.lock().unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())` with a `let` so the recovered state is at least observable, or log on poisoning so a flaky test run is visible in CI logs.

Segment 2 retry loop has no backoff, jitter, or logging. Tight 3-iteration spin against the very contention it tries to paper over — if `llm_integration` U15 is also racing, a busy-spin here amplifies load on `bot-config.json` instead of absorbing it. Consider `std::thread::sleep` with monotonic escalation, and at least surface a warning when the 3rd attempt still fails so silent regression is visible.

The test name advertises coverage of the security-critical 防劫持闸, yet in CI without an embed model the assertion never runs at all. Either inject a deterministic mock embedder (cos = 1.0) so the path is unconditionally exercised, or fail the test (`return`/panic) when the model is missing so the security gap is not invisible.

If anyone flips the test to `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread")]` or the scheduler ever spawns a sub-task that captures the future, the future becomes `Send`-required and this turns into a soundness bug with no compile-time signal. comments.content: DDL is hand-mirrored from `db.rs` because the integration test crate can't reach the private `open_db`. If production schema gains a column, changes a type, or adds a constraint, `upsert_skill_outcome` / `load_all_skill_outcomes` will silently mismatch this DDL — assertions like `row.kind == "done"` and `summary.contains("Step 1")` may pass on stale columns while real persistence drifts with no test failure. Recommend exposing a `pub(crate) fn open_db_in_memory()` (or sharing the DDL via `include_str!` of a single schema file used by both prod and tests) so this DDL can never diverge from production.

Global `intent_router::rebuild_routes(...)` mutation happens before `RoutesResetGuard` is constructed. If `rebuild_routes` or `intent_rules_from_dirs` panics, the global route table is left polluted for subsequent tests in the same binary. `pre_step_pass_through_for_normal_query` does not reset routes and only works because cargo test serializes same-binary tests in a single process by default. Either reset on panic via `std::panic::catch_unwind` wrapping the body, or reset routes in a process-level fixture so the global starts empty for every test regardless of prior-test panic.

The mock executor mutates scheduler-visible `SKILL_RUNS` state mid-flight via `test_hook_insert_skill_run`. The rollback-window assertion (`rollback_states == &[Some(SkillState::Running)]`) therefore depends on the precise internal ordering inside `run_skill_scheduler_core` between (a) step-failure detection, (b) state re-open from Failed→Running, and (c) rollback invocation. Any refactor that caches the state snapshot earlier, or that polls the state on a different cadence, silently breaks this assertion. Prefer a dedicated `test_hook` that records the scheduler's *intent* (a callback fired on re-open/restore) rather than inferring it from external state mutated indirectly by the executor.

`mock_handle()` intentionally leaks a `MockRuntime` per call via `Box::leak`. With ~10 scheduler/middleware tests this leaks ~10 AppHandles reclaimed only at process exit. The scheduler tests do pair `test_hook_insert_skill_run` / `test_hook_remove_skill_run` on `SKILL_RUNS`, which is the obvious candidate to verify. Confirm no other resources ride on the leaked AppHandle (FS handles, channels, spawned threads, or background tasks) that could accumulate or interfere between tests in the same binary — leaked AppHandles with overlapping identifiers could mask or collide in any other `test_hook_*` state keyed off the handle.

Concurrency hazard: `_serial = SERIAL.lock()` is held by the main test task across the entire `duplicate_trigger_rejected_by_exec_guard` test, including while the spawned task (which owns `release_rx`) is alive. The comment block at the top asserts this is safe because `#[tokio::test]` uses a current_thread runtime, but if `run_task_in_chat_with` ever internally `tokio::spawn`s or tries to acquire another `std::sync::Mutex` (e.g. the in-process `ExecGuard` registry) on a worker thread, the spawned task can deadlock waiting for a lock held by the test thread that can never make progress. Either (a) audit that `run_task_in_chat_with` is purely async-without-internal-spawn and uses no std sync mutexes on the ExecGuard path, or (b) use a `tokio::sync::Mutex` and drop the guard between awaits.

PII file written with default umask. std::fs::write creates memory_extract_sample.jsonl using mode 0o666 & ~umask, typically 0o644 on Unix, inside the project tree. The file holds real user memory content, so it is reachable by any process running as the user and by cloud-sync / shared folders. Recommend explicit restrictive mode (e.g. OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true).truncate(true).mode(0o600).custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW) on Unix) or write to a user-only dir (e.g. std::env::temp_dir() with restrictive mode, or $XDG_DATA_HOME/wmessage/eval/).

std::fs::rename does not atomically replace an existing destination on Windows (it returns an error if dst exists), so re-running the test on Windows panics the second time. It also does not preserve the source file's mode on Unix when replacing across the project tree. Use a portable replace helper: remove the destination first (best-effort) and then rename, or use the `atomicwrites` / `tempfile::persist` crate which provides cross-platform atomic replace.

The temp .tmp file is not covered by .gitignore (only fixtures/memory_extract_sample.jsonl is). If the rename fails or the process is killed before rename, the .tmp file containing real user memory content stays in the working tree and can leak through git status / cloud sync / backup tools. Either add `fixtures/memory_extract_sample.jsonl.tmp` (or `*.jsonl.tmp`) to .gitignore, or scope the temp file under a sibling dir already ignored, and clean it up on failure via a defer/guard.

The self-check assert!(r5 > 0.0) does not actually prove the embedding→seed→search chain is alive. hybrid_search_with always includes the 0.20 keyword-overlap term, and the early-return guard in hybrid_score_with only fires when kw == 0.0 AND one side lacks an embedding. As long as the query has any keyword overlap with item content/tags, results can score > 0 even with zero-norm / constant embeddings. Strengthen the assertion by also asserting (a) the top hit's score minus its keyword+importance+recency contribution > some epsilon (proves semantic weight landed), or (b) at least one item.embedding is a finite, non-zero L2 vector, or (c) embed_text returns Some and l2-normalised norm > 0 for a probe string.

comments.content: Setting dedup_merge = 1.0 does not strictly disable semantic merging. insert_item_with uses `if c >= p.dedup_merge`, so two seed vectors with cosine exactly 1.0 (or ≥ 1.0 due to FP rounding of identical L2-normalised embeddings) still trigger the merge branch. The comment claims "关闭语义合并". Either add a dedicated `dedup_disabled: bool` to StoreParams, or use a sentinel like f64::INFINITY (or NaN-checked) so no embedding can ever satisfy the threshold, and short-circuit before the cosine scan.

Aggregate denominator ignores queries outside the fixed CATEGORY_ORDER. per_cat accumulates counts for any q.category string, but the total alln is summed only across the hard-coded CATEGORY_ORDER. If the fixture adds a new or misspelled category, those queries appear in per_cat but are silently dropped from alln, biasing the reported overall recall@1/@5. Either sum across the whole per_cat (BTreeMap values) for alln/all1/all5, or fail loud if any per_cat key is not in CATEGORY_ORDER.

Tied scores can break determinism. hybrid_search_with uses stable sort_by on the score; when two items have identical scores (common here because now, importance and recency are uniform across all seeds, and several seed pairs share only keyword overlap), tie-break order is the iteration order of items. items comes from store::load_all with no ORDER BY, and MemItem.id is a generated UUID, so tie ordering depends on SQLite row enumeration. Either ORDER BY id ASC in load_all (or pass an explicit item order), or add a deterministic secondary sort key (id) in hybrid_search_with.

recall@5 metric name is implicitly coupled to MemoryTuning::default().top_n == 5. If that default ever changes, the test still computes hits.first() correctly, but `recall@5` silently becomes `recall@top_n`. Pass an explicit RankParams { top_n: 5, ..RankParams::of(&MemoryTuning::default()) } so the metric label matches the actual k, and add a debug_assert_eq!(params.top_n, 5) at the top.
